topics.syllabus_excerpt:
Chapter 1 – Matrices and Determinants  
 
School of Mathematical Sciences & Analytics, Singapore Polytechnic Page 1-1  
 
Official (Closed), Non-Sensitive 
Objectives: 
 
1. Define a matrix, its order and elements. 
2. Define some special types of matrices. 
3. Explain transpose of a matrix. 
4. Define and explain the equality rule of matrices. 
5. Perform matrix operations such as addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication and matrix 
multiplication. 
6. Define and evaluate 2nd order determinants. 
7. Define and evaluate higher order determinants. 
8. Use Cramer’s rule to solve simultaneous linear equations with two or three unknowns. 
9. Define the inverse of a square matrix. 
10. Use the inverse matrix method to solve system of linear equations with two unknowns. 
 
 
In our daily life, information can often be conveniently presented as an array of rows and columns. 
Bus timetable and football league results often use this form of presentation. Such an arrangement 
of information is called a matrix. Below are some examples of matrices. 
 
Eg1 The weekly expenditures in dollars of a department for January and February are given 
below. 
January Week Payroll Marketing Miscellaneous 
 1 10000 5000 500 
 2 10000 3000 400 
 3 10000 4000 300 
 4 10000 6000 600 
 
February Week Payroll Marketing Miscellaneous 
 1 12000 6000 700 
 2 12000 3000 300 
 3 12000 5000 500 
 4 12000 4000 200 
Matrix addition can be used to find the total expenditures for the three categories Payroll, 
Marketing and Miscellaneous during the corresponding weeks of January and February. 
 
 
Eg2 A building contractor accepts summer orders for 135 houses, 3 condominiums and 1 high 
rise building. The construction materials (in appropriate units) that go into each of these 
buildings are listed in the table below. Using matrices, we can find how much of each 
raw material will be needed for all the summer contracts. 
 
Material House Condominium High rise 
Lumber 10 400 500 
Glass 5 150 1000 
Steel 0 50 2000 
Concrete 0 100 1000 
Labour 20 1000 5000

The goal of this series of problem-solving assignments is to develop problem-solving skills, not 
just to test your ability to get the answer. It’s ok to try hard and not succeed at first (only your 
effort is evaluated), but you must try.  
 
Question 
At the beginning of 2017, a customer invested a total of $100,000 in four investment plans : A, B, 
C and D. At the end of 2017, the amount of profit he made from plans A, B and C are 2%, 3% and 
6% respectively, giving a total  profit of $4000. He made a loss of 6% in plan D , which is $900. 
The amount of money invested in plan B is twice the amount of money invested in plan A.

3.1 Introduction 
 
Many real-world phenomena involve changing quantities – the speed of a vehicle, the inflation of 
currency, the number of bacteria in a culture, the voltage of an electrical signal, and so forth.  In this 
chapter, we will cover the concept of a “derivative” or “differentiation”, which is the mathematical 
tool for studying the rate at which one quantity changes relative to another.  This is closely related 
to the geometric concept of a tangent line to a curve, which will be used to introduce the derivative.

4.3.1 Implicit Functions 
 
So far, we have dealt mostly with explicit functions in the topics we have covered. 
 
Explicit functions are those functions whereby one variable (usually  y) can be isolated and 
expressed clearly in terms of the other variables (usually  x).

5.5.1 Increasing and Decreasing Functions 
 
A function is said to be increasing when its graph rises as it goes from left to right.  A 
function is decreasing when its graph falls as it goes from left to right.  The

5.5.2 Maximum and Minimum Points 
 
When a graph of a continuous function changes from rising to falling, a relative maximum 
occurs, and when the graph changes from falling to rising, a relative minimum occurs.

when ()fx′  is not defined.  They are points D and F.  The slope of the tangent line is not 
defined at such points as the tangent line is either vertical or does not exist.

One very important application of differential calculus is the solving of maximum-minimum 
problems.  In this section, we shall look at how the methods can be used to solve some 
applied optimisation problems. 
 
Suggested Steps for Solving Applied Optimisation Problems: 
1 Read the problem carefully. Where relevant and possible, sketch a diagram. 
2 Label the diagram with appropriate variables and constants to show the relationships 
between them.  
3 Identify the quantity which is to be optimised and call it Q. 
4 Translate the problem to a mathematical equation involving Q.  
5 Express Q as a function of one variable only, say, x. For that to happen, sometimes you 
may need to make substitutions.   
6 Find the derivative 
dQ
dx . 
7 Set the derivative to zero and solve for x. 
8 Determine the desired maximum or minimum value using the techniques introduced in 
the preceding sections. 
 
 
Example 12 : A rectangular area is to be enclosed using an existing wall as one side and 
100m of fencing for the other three sides. What would be the necessary 
dimensions of the enclosure so that the area is the maximum possible?

questions.question:
A horse feeder is a hollow open-topped triangular prism as shown. Its vertical triangular end faces are isosceles right triangles: $AB=BC=DE=EF$, $\angle ABC=\angle DEF=90^\circ$. Edges are horizontal, $AC=x$ m, and capacity is $4$ m$^3$.
(a) Show its external surface area is $A=\frac12x^2+16\sqrt2/x$ m$^2$. (b) Find the exact $x$ giving optimum $A$, state its nature, and express $x$ as $k\sqrt2$ for integer $k$. (c) Find the optimum area.
questions.solution:
(a) Each triangle has area $\frac12(x/\sqrt2)^2=x^2/4$. With prism length $h$, $x^2h/4=4$, so $h=16/x^2$. Thus $A=2(x^2/4)+2(x/\sqrt2)h=x^2/2+16\sqrt2/x$.
(b) $A'=x-16\sqrt2/x^2=0$ gives $x^3=16\sqrt2$, hence $x=2\sqrt2$. $A''=1+32\sqrt2/x^3=3>0$, a minimum.
(c) $A(2\sqrt2)=12$ m$^2$.
questions.alternative_solution_1: Alternative first step in (a): triangle area $=\frac12 x(x/2)=x^2/4$. Continue as in the main solution.

questions.question: The curve shown has gradient $dy/dx=6-4x$, passes through $(0,0)$, and has maximum point $B$. (a) Find its equation. (b) Find the shaded area bounded by the curve, the $x$ axis and line $AB$.
questions.solution:
(a) $y=\int(6-4x)dx=6x-2x^2+C$. Through $(0,0)$ gives $C=0$.
(b) At $B$, $6-4x=0$, so $B=(3/2,9/2)$. Triangle area below $AB$ is $\frac12(3/2)(9/2)=27/8$. Curve roots are $0,3$. Area under the curve from $1.5$ to $3$ is $[3x^2-2x^3/3]_{1.5}^3=9/2$. Total shaded area $=27/8+9/2=63/8=7.875$ square units.
questions.alternative_solution_1: For (b), use symmetry of roots $0,3$ to obtain the maximum at $x=(0+3)/2=3/2$. The line is $y=3x$ and its area is $\int_0^{3/2}3x\,dx=27/8$. Add $\int_{3/2}^3(6x-2x^2)dx=9/2$ to give $63/8$.

questions.question: Let $z$ be complex with $|z|=1$ and $z^4+1/z^4=2$. (a) Show $\arg z=n\pi/2$ for integer $n$. (b) Deduce an expression for $z+1/z$ in terms of cosine.
questions.solution:
(a) Put $z=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta$. De Moivre gives $z^4=\cos4\theta+j\sin4\theta$. Rationalising the reciprocal gives $z^{-4}=\cos4\theta-j\sin4\theta$. Thus $2\cos4\theta=2$, so $4\theta=2n\pi$ and $\theta=n\pi/2$.
(b) Rationalising $1/z$ gives $\cos\theta-j\sin\theta$, hence $z+1/z=2\cos\theta$.
questions.alternative_solution_1: (a) Write $z=1\angle\theta$. Then $z^4+z^{-4}=1\angle4\theta+1\angle(-4\theta)=2\cos4\theta=2$, so $\theta=n\pi/2$. (b) As in main solution, $z+1/z=2\cos\theta$.

questions.question: A man in a rowboat at $O$ is 3 km from the nearest shoreline point $A$. Town $C$ is 10 km along the shore from $A$. He rows to $B$ on the shore, then walks to $C$. Let $AB=x$ km. He rows at 2.5 km/h and walks at 4 km/h. (a) Find $OB$ using Pythagoras. (b) Where should $B$ be to minimise travel time? Hint: distance = speed $\times$ time.
questions.solution: (a) $OB=\sqrt{x^2+9}$ km. (b) $T=\sqrt{x^2+9}/2.5+(10-x)/4$. Then $T'=x/(2.5\sqrt{x^2+9})-1/4$. Setting $T'=0$ gives $4x=2.5\sqrt{x^2+9}$, $9.75x^2=56.25$, $x^2=75/13$. Thus $x=2.40$ km (negative root rejected). $T''=\frac1{2.5}\frac{\sqrt{x^2+9}-x(2x/(2\sqrt{x^2+9}))}{x^2+9}>0$, so this is a minimum.

questions.question: Given $\overline z=9/z$ and $\arg(4\overline z/(-j))=-5\pi/12$. (a) Find $z$ in exponential form. (b) Find real $a,b$, $-\pi<b\le\pi$, such that $e^{3a}\times e^{\ln[e^{jb}]}=z^2$. Hint: $e^{\ln f(x)}=f(x)$.
questions.solution:
(a) Let $z=x+jy$. Then $x^2+y^2=9$ and $4\overline z/(-j)=4y+j4x$. The source writes $\tan(5\pi/12)=|4x/(4y)|$, then $3.732y=x$. Using the quadrant, it obtains $y=0.7765$, $x=-2.898$, hence $z=3e^{j2.88}$.
(b) $z^2=9e^{j11\pi/6}=9e^{-j\pi/6}=e^{3a}e^{jb}$. Therefore $a=(\ln9)/3$ and $b=-\pi/6$.
questions.alternative_solution_1: (a) Let $z=r\angle\theta$. Since $z\overline z=9$, $r=3$. The argument condition gives $-\theta+\pi/2=-5\pi/12$, so $\theta=11\pi/12$ and $z=3e^{j11\pi/12}$. (b) Then $z^2=9e^{-j\pi/6}$ and $a=(\ln9)/3$, $b=-\pi/6$.

questions.question: Show that $\frac{e^{j\theta}}{e^{j\theta}-1}=\frac12-\frac j2\cot(\theta/2)$.
questions.solution:
Multiply numerator and denominator by $e^{-j\theta}-1$:
$\frac{e^{j\theta}}{e^{j\theta}-1}=\frac{1-e^{j\theta}}{2-(e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta})}=\frac{1-\cos\theta-j\sin\theta}{2(1-\cos\theta)}$
$=\frac12-\frac{j\sin\theta}{2(1-\cos\theta)}=\frac12-\frac{j\,2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)}{4\sin^2(\theta/2)}=\frac12-\frac j2\cot(\theta/2)$.
questions.alternative_solution_1: Multiply numerator and denominator by $e^{-j\theta/2}$. Then the ratio equals $e^{j\theta/2}/(e^{j\theta/2}-e^{-j\theta/2})=[\cos(\theta/2)+j\sin(\theta/2)]/[2j\sin(\theta/2)]=1/2+\cot(\theta/2)/(2j)=1/2-(j/2)\cot(\theta/2)$.

questions.question: A rectangle is inscribed in a semicircle of radius 10 cm. Its width is $2x$ cm, $0<x<10$, and height $h$ cm, as shown. (a) Express its perimeter $P$ in terms of $x$ only. (b) Find maximum $P$. (c) Find the rectangle's width and height.
questions.solution:
(a) $x^2+h^2=100$, so $h=\sqrt{100-x^2}$ and $P=4x+2\sqrt{100-x^2}$.
(b) $P'=4-2x/\sqrt{100-x^2}=0$ gives $2\sqrt{100-x^2}=x$, $5x^2=400$, $x=4\sqrt5$ (negative rejected). Thus $P=20\sqrt5\approx44.7$ cm. $P''=-200(100-x^2)^{-3/2}<0$, so this is a maximum.
(c) $h=2\sqrt5\approx4.47$ cm; width $=8\sqrt5\approx17.9$ cm.

questions.question:
The curves $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$, $0\le x\le\pi/2$, intersect at $P=(\pi/4,1/\sqrt2)$. $A_1$ is bounded by the curves and $x$ axis, and $A_2$ by the curves and $y$ axis, as shown.
(a) Find $A_1,A_2$ exactly or to 3 s.f. (b) A vertical line $x=a$ divides $A_1$ in ratio $1:2$, with the smaller part to its left. Find $a$ in radians. Show all workings.
questions.solution:
(a) $A_1=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin x\,dx+\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx=2-\sqrt2\approx0.586$ square units. $A_2=\int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x-\sin x)dx=\sqrt2-1\approx0.414$ square units.
(b) $(2-\sqrt2)/3=\int_0^a\sin x\,dx=1-\cos a$. Thus $\cos a=(1+\sqrt2)/3$ and $a=0.635$ rad.
questions.alternative_solution_1: Alternative (b): $\frac{\int_0^a\sin x\,dx}{\int_a^{\pi/4}\sin x\,dx+\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx}=1/2$. Hence $(1-\cos a)/(1+\cos a-\sqrt2)=1/2$, giving $3\cos a=1+\sqrt2$ and $a=0.635$ rad. Part (a) as main solution.

questions.question: Let $Z^3+(\overline Z)^3=8$ and $|Z|=2$. Find all $Z$ in exponential form with $-\pi/3<\arg Z\le\pi/3$.
questions.solution: Write $Z=2e^{j\theta}$, $\overline Z=2e^{-j\theta}$. Then $Z^3+\overline Z^3=8e^{j3\theta}+8e^{-j3\theta}=16\cos3\theta=8$, so $\cos3\theta=1/2$. Since $-\pi<3\theta\le\pi$, $3\theta=\pm\pi/3$, hence $\theta=\pm\pi/9$. Thus $Z=2e^{j\pi/9}$ or $2e^{-j\pi/9}$.

questions.question: Given $z+w=|z|w$, where $z,w$ are complex numbers and $|w|>1$, find $|z|$ in terms of $|w|$.
questions.alternative_solution_1: $|z|-1=z/w=z\overline w/(w\overline w)$, so $(|z|-1)|w|^2=z\overline w$. Let $z=x+jy$, $w=a+jb$. The right side is $xa+by+j(ya-bx)$; hence $ya=bx$. Therefore $(xa+by)^2=(x^2+y^2)(a^2+b^2)=|z|^2|w|^2$, giving $xa+by=\pm|z||w|$. Substitution gives $|z|=|w|/(|w|-1)$ or $|w|/(|w|+1)$.
questions.alternative_solution_2: Write $z=r_z\angle\theta_z$ and $w=r_w\angle\theta_w$. Equating real and imaginary parts gives $r_z\cos\theta_z=r_w\cos\theta_w(r_z-1)$ and $r_z\sin\theta_z=r_w\sin\theta_w(r_z-1)$. The source divides these to obtain $\tan\theta_w=\tan\theta_z$. For equal directions, $r_z+r_w=r_zr_w$, giving $r_z=r_w/(r_w-1)$. For opposite directions, $-r_z+r_w=r_zr_w$, giving $r_z=r_w/(r_w+1)$.
questions.alternative_solution_3: Let $z=re^{j\theta}$, $w=Re^{j\phi}$. Then $re^{j\theta}=Re^{j\phi}(r-1)$, so $r=R|r-1|$. If $r\ge1$, $r=R(r-1)$ and $r=R/(R-1)$. If $r<1$, $r=R(1-r)$ and $r=R/(1+R)$.

questions.question: Given $2Z+\overline{jZ}=6$, where $Z=x+jy$ for real $x,y$: (i) solve for $Z$; (ii) plot $Z$ and $\overline Z$ on the same Argand diagram, clearly labelling axes and coordinates.
questions.solution: $2(x+jy)+\overline{j(x+jy)}=6$. Since $\overline{j(x+jy)}=-y-jx$, equating real and imaginary parts gives $2x-y=6$ and $2y-x=0$. Hence $x=4$, $y=2$, $Z=4+2j$ and $\overline Z=4-2j$. Plot $Z$ at $(4,2)$ and $\overline Z$ at $(4,-2)$ on the Argand diagram, with horizontal real and vertical imaginary axes.

questions.question:
(a) Given $D=\begin{pmatrix}5&3&0.5\\4&2.5&2\\3&2&1.5\end{pmatrix}$, $E=\begin{pmatrix}1&14&-19\\0&-24&32\\-2&4&-2\end{pmatrix}$. (i) Find $DE$. (ii) Hence find $D^{-1}$.
(b) A cafe makes Bread Loaf, Cake and Muffin. Rows of $D$ give their flour, butter and sugar requirements in hundreds of grams. A supplier charges \$0.20, \$1.35 and \$0.25 per 100 g respectively. (i) Write two matrices whose product gives unit production costs. (ii) Find those costs to the nearest cent. (iii) With a new supplier, unit production costs become \$4.95, \$4.67 and \$3.63 without recipe changes. Using (a), find the new price per 100 g for each ingredient, to the nearest cent.
questions.solution:
(a) $DE=4I$, so $D^{-1}=E/4$.
(b)(i) Multiply $D$ by $F=\begin{pmatrix}0.20\\1.35\\0.25\end{pmatrix}$. (ii) $DF\approx\begin{pmatrix}5.18\\4.68\\3.68\end{pmatrix}$ dollars. (iii) $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=D^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}4.95\\4.67\\3.63\end{pmatrix}=\frac14E\begin{pmatrix}4.95\\4.67\\3.63\end{pmatrix}\approx\begin{pmatrix}0.34\\1.02\\0.38\end{pmatrix}$ dollars per 100 g.
questions.alternative_solution_1: For (b)(i)-(ii), use the row vector $F=(0.20\;1.35\;0.25)$ and the transpose of the ingredient matrix: $FD^T\approx(5.18\;4.68\;3.68)$. Other parts use the main solution.

questions.sub_topic: The Exponential Form of a Complex Number
questions.question: Let $z_1=j$ and $z_2=re^{j\theta}$ be nonzero complex numbers, with real $r,\theta$ and $r>0$. Given $z=z_1z_2$, show for any positive integer $n$ that $z^n+\overline{z^n}=Ar^n\cos[n(B+\theta)]$, where $A,B$ are positive real constants to determine.
questions.solution: $z=jre^{j\theta}$, so $z^n=j^nr^ne^{jn\theta}=r^ne^{jn(\pi/2+\theta)}$. Its conjugate is $r^ne^{-jn(\pi/2+\theta)}$. Adding and expanding Euler's formula cancels imaginary parts, giving $2r^n\cos[n(\pi/2+\theta)]$. Thus $A=2$, $B=\pi/2$.
questions.alternative_solution_1: In polar form, $z=j(r\angle\theta)$, hence $z^n=r^n\angle n(\pi/2+\theta)$ and $\overline{z^n}=r^n\angle[-n(\pi/2+\theta)]$. Adding the rectangular forms gives $2r^n\cos[n(\pi/2+\theta)]$, so $A=2$, $B=\pi/2$.

questions.question: Solve for real $x,y$: $4x-jy+1=j2+5/(2+j)$.
questions.solution: $4x-jy+1-j2=\frac5{2+j}\frac{2-j}{2-j}=2-j$. Real parts: $4x+1=2\Rightarrow x=1/4$. Imaginary parts: $-y-2=-1\Rightarrow y=-1$.
questions.alternative_solution_1: Multiply by $2+j$: $(4x-jy+1-j2)(2+j)=5$. Equating components gives $8x+y+4=5$ and $-2y+4x-3=0$. Thus $y=1-8x$, $20x=5$, $x=1/4$, $y=-1$.

questions.question:
(a) Let $D=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&1\\2&4&2\\1&1&3\end{pmatrix}$. (i) Show $D^2-8D+12I=O$, where $I,O$ are $3\times3$ identity and zero matrices. (ii) Hence find $D^{-1}$.
(b) A startup makes P-Phone, T-Tablet and W-Watch. Their material quantities (earth catalyst in mg, super-conductor in cm, graphene heat shield in square inches) and assembly costs in dollars are
\[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}\text{P-Phone}&0.250&0.500&0.250&6\\\text{T-Tablet}&0.125&0.125&0.375&8\\\text{W-Watch}&0.375&0.125&0.125&3\end{array}\]
Total costs per gadget are \$45, \$50, \$35 respectively. Using (a)(ii) and matrix methods, find each material's unit cost to the nearest cent.
questions.solution:
(a)(i) $D^2=\begin{pmatrix}12&8&8\\16&20&16\\8&8&12\end{pmatrix}$, so $D^2-8D+12I=O$. (ii) Multiplying by $D^{-1}$ gives $D-8I+12D^{-1}=O$, so $D^{-1}=\frac1{12}(8I-D)=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}5&-1&-1\\-2&4&-2\\-1&-1&5\end{pmatrix}$.
(b) Subtract assembly costs from totals, then reorder equations: $\frac18D\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}32\\39\\42\end{pmatrix}$. Hence $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=D^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}256\\312\\336\end{pmatrix}\approx\begin{pmatrix}52.67\\5.33\\92.67\end{pmatrix}$. Costs are \$52.67/mg, \$5.33/cm and \$92.67/square inch.
